segments.narration: Nevada drilled for power and accidentally built a geyser. Fly Ranch, in the desert west of the Black Rock. It has not stopped since 1964.
A geothermal company sank a well there, found the water too cool to be worth anything, and capped it off. The seal failed.
Hot water has been pushing out of it ever since, loaded with dissolved calcium carbonate and silica. And every litre leaves a little of that behind.
So it is still growing. Mineral cones, stepped pools, a mound now roughly thirty feet, built by a mistake nobody fixed.
The scarlet and green are heat-loving microbes living in the runoff. In 2016 Burning Man's nonprofit bought the entire ranch, geyser included, for six and a half million dollars.

verdicts.claim: A geothermal company drilled a well there in 1964, found the water not hot enough to use, reportedly capped it, and the seal failed.

verdicts.claim: The escaping water carries dissolved calcium carbonate and silica, which it deposits around the vent.
verdicts.note: Both sources name calcium carbonate and silica as the minerals building up around the new vent.

verdicts.claim: Those deposits built the geyser's cones and travertine pools, with the whole mound reported at roughly 25 to 30 feet.
verdicts.note: The 25-30 ft (7.6-9.1 m) mound figure appears in Wikipedia's origin section and in WorldAtlas; Wikipedia's lead gives a smaller figure for the cone alone, which is why the narration says 'the whole structure' and gives no jet height.

verdicts.claim: The green and red colours come from thermophilic microbes, and the Burning Man Project bought the 3,800-acre Fly Ranch in June 2016 for $6.5 million.
